description: On November 5, 2026, AI chip stocks had their worst day since 2020 and about $3 trillion of market value vanished. Why it happened, how rare it was, and what came next after every 10% chip crash since 2000. Plus: $10 a day in Nvidia since ChatGPT launched.
- CNBC and Reuters via StockTitan: Nov 5–6, 2026 market moves
- Yahoo Finance live coverage, Nov 6, 2026 (market value, Goldman Sachs data center estimate, jobs report)
- Daily price data: Yahoo Finance (PHLX Semiconductor Index, NVDA, AMD, MU, INTC, AVGO, SOXX, SPY)
Past crashes do not predict the future. Not financial advice. For education only.

segments.vo: Three trillion dollars. Gone in one day.

On Thursday, November fifth, the Nasdaq fell five and a half percent. The S and P five hundred, more than four. Its worst day since the tariff crash of April 2025. Yahoo Finance put the damage at about three trillion dollars of market value.
And the AI chip stocks got destroyed. Micron, {MU_d1_words}. AMD, {AMD_d1_words}. Intel, {INTC_d1_words}. Broadcom, {AVGO_d1_words}. Even Nvidia, {NVDA_d1_words}, in a single day.

So what happened? Is the AI boom over? And stay to the end, because I went back and checked every single day chip stocks crashed ten percent or more since the year 2000, to see what happened next. The answer surprised me.
Here's the trigger. On election night, Democrats won control of Congress.

Investors started betting that new rules could slow down the thing powering the whole AI trade. Data centers. And this isn't just one party. Candidates on both sides had campaigned against giant data centers, over power bills, water and land. Goldman Sachs estimated that about forty-five percent of planned US data center capacity could face restrictions.

scene.source: Goldman Sachs estimate via Yahoo Finance

segments.vo: Why does that matter so much? Because AI chips don't sell themselves. Every data center is a giant order for chips, memory and power gear. Slow the buildings, and you slow the orders. That's why memory makers like Micron got hit even harder than Nvidia.

Because the very next day, Friday, chip stocks bounced. AMD up about eleven percent. Intel up almost eight. The jobs report came in hot, at a hundred sixty-five thousand jobs. Jefferies called Thursday's selloff reactionary, not a fundamental reset.
Okay. Time for the data. How rare was Thursday for chip stocks?
The Philadelphia semiconductor index, the scoreboard for chip stocks, fell about {sox1_pct} in one day. The last time it dropped that much? {sox1_last}.

Now here's the part most headlines skip. Since the year 2000, the chip index has crashed ten percent or more in one day {panic_count_words}. Not once. {panic_count_words}. So I checked what happened next, every time.
One month after a crash day, chip stocks were on average {panic_m1_avg_words}. And one year later? On average {panic_y1_avg_words}. Up in {panic_y1_up} cases.

segments.vo: Think about what that means. On the day of every one of those crashes, the headlines said the same thing you're hearing now. The boom is over. Get out. Sometimes they were right for a while. But a year later, more often than not, the people who sold in the panic were the ones who regretted it.

segments.vo: But careful. The crash days come in clusters, mostly during 2000 to 2002 and 2008, when it took years to recover. The worst one was {panic_worst}, {panic_worst_words}. A crash day tells you fear is high. It does not tell you the bottom is in.
And now, the moment I promised. Say you put ten dollars into Nvidia every single trading day, starting the day ChatGPT launched, November thirtieth, 2022. Crash included.
You'd have put in {bt_invested}. Even after Thursday, it's worth {bt_value}. That's {bt_return_words}. Your worst moment? On {bt_dd_date}, you were {bt_dd_words} from your peak.

Read that again. Even buying every day through the hype, the crashes, and this week's panic, the slow and boring plan still came out ahead. Not because anyone timed the bottom. Because they kept buying when it felt terrible.

Same ten dollars a day, same start date. AMD? {AMD_dca_value}, {AMD_dca_words}. Micron? {MU_dca_value}, {MU_dca_words}. And a boring S and P five hundred fund? {SPY_dca_value}, {SPY_dca_words}. So which bet paid the most? {dca_winner}.

One more twist. March sixteenth, 2020. The worst day of the COVID crash. Stocks were in free fall and everyone wanted out. Say you bought ten thousand dollars of chip stocks, through the chip fund SOXX, that day. Today that's worth {panic2020_value}. That's {panic2020_change_words}.
So what happens next? We don't predict. But here are three ways this goes.

scene.sub: No predictions. Just what to watch.

segments.vo: One. Blip. Thursday was panic, the data center orders keep coming, and chips grind back. Two. Grind. New rules slow some projects, and chips drift sideways for months. Three. Reset. Spending really slows, and like 2000 or 2008, the drops come in clusters. Watch three things. Nvidia's earnings later this month. Any new data center bills. And whether big tech keeps its spending plans.
